126257.m: Giacomo Rizzolatti discovered mirror neurons in Parma.

126258.q: During which action by macaques were mirror neurons first noticed?
126258.e: The cells in the premotor area F5 fired when a monkey reached for food and also when it watched a human reaching.
126258.m: Mirror neurons were discovered during grasping movements.

126259.q: What is special about mirror neurons?
a: They fire both when doing and when watching an action
They reflect light like a mirror
126259.e: Mirror neurons are active when a monkey reaches for something itself and when it sees others doing the same. Watching and doing are linked in this way.
126259.m: Mirror neurons react to your own actions and to actions you watch.

126260.q: In which decade were mirror neurons first described?
126260.e: The first publications appeared in the 1990s. Since then, mirror neurons have been studied and debated intensively.
126260.m: Mirror neurons were described in the 1990s.

126261.q: According to widespread hypotheses, which abilities are mirror neurons said to support?
126261.e: It is thought that mirror neurons help us to understand and copy other people’s actions. A link with compassion is also being discussed.
126261.m: Mirror neurons are linked with imitation and empathy.

126262.q: Why is the role of mirror neurons in humans disputed?
a: Direct measurements of single cells are rare
Humans have no nerve cells at all
They have only been found in computer models
126262.e: In humans, most evidence comes from indirect methods such as brain imaging. Recordings from single cells are only rarely possible, for example during operations.
126262.m: There are only a few direct measurements of mirror neurons in humans.

126263.q: Which human language area is seen as a possible equivalent of area F5 in macaques?
126263.e: Broca’s area in the frontal lobe is involved in producing speech. Because it might correspond to area F5, some suspect a link between mirror neurons and language.
126263.m: Broca’s area is seen as the human equivalent of area F5.

126264.q: What does a brain-computer interface make possible?
a: Controlling devices with brain activity alone
126264.e: A brain-computer interface measures brain signals and translates them into commands for devices. Muscles and nerves are bypassed.
126264.m: A brain-computer interface translates brain signals into commands.

126265.q: Which non-invasive measuring method is used most often in brain-computer interfaces?
126265.e: In electroencephalography, EEG for short, electrodes on the scalp measure brain waves. No operation is needed.
126265.m: EEG measures brain waves without an operation.

126266.q: Why do electrodes implanted in the brain give more accurate signals than electrodes on the scalp?
a: They measure right at the nerve cells, without the skull and skin muffling the signal
They have their own battery in the head
126266.e: The skull bone and skin weaken and blur the electrical signals. Implanted electrodes, on the other hand, can pick up the activity of single nerve cells.
126266.m: Implanted electrodes measure more accurately than EEG.

126267.q: Which research project allowed paralysed people with brain implants to control a computer cursor?
126267.e: In the BrainGate project, electrodes were implanted in the motor cortex of paralysed people. With them, they could move cursors and robotic arms.
126267.m: BrainGate helped paralysed people control computers with their thoughts.

126268.q: Who can brain-computer interfaces especially help?
a: People who are paralysed and cannot speak
126268.e: With complete paralysis, the brain often still works, but the signals do not reach the muscles. An interface can turn brain signals directly into letters or movements.
126268.m: Brain-computer interfaces give paralysed people new possibilities.

126269.q: What did researchers at EPFL and CHUV in Lausanne achieve with a “digital bridge” between brain and spinal cord?
a: A paralysed man was able to walk again
A blind man was able to read again
A deaf man was able to hear music
A patient was able to send thoughts
126269.e: Implants read the intention to move in the brain and stimulate the spinal cord below the injury. A man paralysed from the waist down was able to take some steps again.
126269.m: A digital bridge from Lausanne helped a paralysed man to walk.

126270.q: Which mental strategy do many EEG-based brain-computer interfaces use?
126270.e: If you imagine moving your left or right hand, the activity over the motor cortex changes. A computer can tell these patterns apart.
126270.m: Imagined movements produce measurable brain signals.

126271.q: What disadvantage do invasive brain-computer interfaces have compared with EEG?
126271.e: Implanted electrodes give more accurate signals but have to be put in by surgery. This brings risks such as infections.
126271.m: Invasive interfaces need an operation on the brain.

126272.q: Who mainly funded the Human Brain Project?
126272.e: The Human Brain Project was one of the EU’s flagship projects for future technologies. Hundreds of researchers from many countries worked on it.
126272.m: The Human Brain Project was an EU flagship project.

126273.q: Roughly how long did the Human Brain Project run?
126273.e: The project started in 2013 and ended in 2023. It was planned from the start to last about a decade.
126273.m: The Human Brain Project ran for about ten years.

126274.q: Which neuroscientist is seen as the initiator of the Human Brain Project?
126274.e: Henry Markram promoted the vision of simulating the human brain on a computer. He led the project in its early days.
126274.m: Henry Markram launched the Human Brain Project.

126275.q: Which Swiss university coordinated the Human Brain Project in its early phase?
126275.e: The École polytechnique fédérale de Lausanne was the coordinating institution at the beginning. Later the leadership was reorganised.
126275.m: EPFL coordinated the Human Brain Project at first.

126276.q: What means did the Human Brain Project mainly want to use to study the brain?
126276.e: The project relied on supercomputers, digital brain models and detailed atlases of the brain. Data from many laboratories was meant to be brought together in this way.
126276.m: The Human Brain Project studied the brain with simulations and atlases.

126277.q: What sparked a big controversy about the Human Brain Project in 2014?
a: An open letter from critical researchers
A fire in the data centre
126277.e: Many neuroscientists criticised the direction and management of the project in an open letter. Afterwards the leadership was restructured.
126277.m: An open letter sparked criticism of the Human Brain Project in 2014.

126278.q: Which research infrastructure is a lasting result of the Human Brain Project?
126278.e: EBRAINS gives researchers digital access to data, brain atlases and simulation tools. The platform continues after the end of the project.
126278.m: EBRAINS is the lasting legacy of the Human Brain Project.

126279.q: What budget was the Human Brain Project originally planned with?
126279.e: The project was planned to cost about one billion euros. A large part came from the EU, the rest from the countries involved.
126279.m: The Human Brain Project was planned with about one billion euros.

126280.q: What did Alois Alzheimer find in 1906 in the brain of his patient who had died?
a: Deposits between nerve cells and bundles of fibres inside them
126280.e: Alzheimer examined the brain of Auguste Deter. He described plaques and bundles of fibrils, which are still seen today as typical signs of the disease.
126280.m: Plaques and fibre bundles are the hallmarks of Alzheimer’s disease.

126281.q: Which protein are the plaques that build up between nerve cells in Alzheimer’s disease made of?
126281.e: Beta-amyloid clumps together outside the nerve cells into plaques. They are among the typical signs of the disease.
126281.m: Alzheimer’s plaques are made of beta-amyloid.

126282.q: Which protein forms the bundles of fibrils inside the nerve cells in Alzheimer’s disease?
126282.e: Tau protein normally stabilises the cell’s skeleton. In Alzheimer’s disease it changes and clumps into fibrils that damage the cell.
126282.m: In Alzheimer’s disease, tau protein clumps inside the nerve cells.

126283.q: Where does Alzheimer’s disease stand among the forms of dementia?
a: It is the most common form
It is a very rare form
It is not a form of dementia
126283.e: Alzheimer’s disease causes about two thirds of all cases of dementia. Other forms include vascular dementia, for example.
126283.m: Alzheimer’s is the most common cause of dementia.

126284.q: What is the biggest known risk factor for Alzheimer’s disease?
126284.e: The risk rises clearly with age. Most people affected are over 65.
126284.m: Age is the biggest risk factor for Alzheimer’s.

126285.q: How do many medicines used for mild to moderate Alzheimer’s dementia work?
a: They slow down the breakdown of acetylcholine
126285.e: These medicines slow down the breakdown of the messenger acetylcholine. This can ease symptoms for a while but does not cure the disease.
126285.m: Many Alzheimer’s medicines make acetylcholine work for longer.

126286.q: What role do genes play in the common, late-onset form of Alzheimer’s disease?
a: Certain gene variants increase the risk but do not definitely cause it
Genes play no part in it
A single gene causes it in every case
It is only inherited from the mother
126286.e: The best-known risk variant is ApoE4. People who carry it develop the disease more often, but not necessarily.
126286.m: Gene variants such as ApoE4 increase the risk of Alzheimer’s.

126287.q: Which memory ability is usually affected first in Alzheimer’s disease?
126287.e: Typically, at the beginning, new events are quickly forgotten. Old memories and well-practised movements often last longer.
126287.m: In Alzheimer’s, remembering new things suffers first.

126288.q: Is there a treatment that cures Alzheimer’s disease (as of 2026)?
a: No, only relief and slowing down
Yes, an operation on the heart
126288.e: Existing medicines can ease symptoms, and newer antibodies can slow the course a little. A cure is not yet possible.
126288.m: Alzheimer’s cannot be cured so far.

126289.q: What job did Phineas Gage have at the time of his accident?
a: Foreman on a railway construction gang
126289.e: In 1848, near Cavendish in Vermont, Phineas Gage was in charge of blasting work for building a railway line. That is when his famous accident happened.
126289.m: Phineas Gage was a foreman in railway construction.

126290.q: In which year did Phineas Gage’s accident happen?
126290.e: The accident happened in September 1848 in the USA. It became one of the best-known cases in brain research.
126290.m: Phineas Gage had his accident in 1848.

126291.q: Which object pierced Phineas Gage’s skull in the explosion?
126291.e: While he was packing down blasting powder, a spark set off the charge. The long tamping rod was shot through his cheek and the top of his skull.
126291.m: An iron tamping rod went through Phineas Gage’s head.

126292.q: Which part of Phineas Gage’s brain was mainly injured in the accident?
126292.e: The rod went in below the left eye and came out at the top of the skull. Above all, the left front part of the frontal lobe was destroyed.
126292.m: In Phineas Gage, mainly the left frontal lobe was injured.

126293.q: Which change was reported in Phineas Gage after the accident?
126293.e: Friends reported that after the accident Gage was moody and had no self-control. They said he was “no longer Gage”.
126293.m: The accident changed Phineas Gage’s personality.

126294.q: Why is the case of Phineas Gage so important for brain research?
a: It showed that the frontal lobe helps shape personality
It proved that the brain is unimportant for behaviour
It showed that the cerebellum controls language
It led to the invention of the X-ray
126294.e: After his frontal lobe was injured, Gage’s behaviour changed greatly. The case was an early sign that certain brain regions influence personality and self-control.
126294.m: The Gage case showed the role of the frontal lobe in personality.

126295.q: How long did Phineas Gage live after his accident?
126295.e: Gage survived the serious injury and died in May 1860. During this time he was able to work again and earn his own living.
126295.m: Phineas Gage lived for about twelve years after the accident.

126296.q: A few years after his accident, Phineas Gage worked as a stagecoach driver. What do researchers conclude from this today?
a: He had partly recovered from his injury
He had not suffered any brain damage at all
He had lost his memory completely
He had already been a coachman before the accident
126296.e: Gage drove stagecoaches in Chile for about seven years. This demanding work suggests that he had partly recovered and adapted.

126297.q: Which federal law regulates compulsory health insurance in Switzerland?
126297.e: The Federal Health Insurance Act (KVG) sets out who must be insured and which services basic insurance pays for.
126297.m: Basic insurance is based on the Health Insurance Act.

126298.q: Since which year has health insurance been compulsory throughout Switzerland?
126298.e: The Health Insurance Act was accepted in a popular vote in 1994 and came into force on 1 January 1996. Since then, everyone living in Switzerland must be insured.
126298.m: Basic insurance has been compulsory for everyone since 1996.

126299.q: Within what period must a person take out health insurance after moving to Switzerland?
126299.e: Anyone moving to Switzerland must take out insurance within three months. The insurance then applies retroactively from the date of arrival.
126299.m: After moving here, you have three months to get insured.

126300.q: What are health insurers not allowed to do in basic insurance?
a: Reject a person because of previous illnesses
Set different premiums for premium regions
126300.e: In basic insurance, there is an obligation to accept: every insurer must accept every person regardless of age and state of health.
126300.m: In basic insurance, every insurer must accept everyone.

126301.q: Which of these does the basic insurance premium not depend on?
126301.e: Basic insurance has per-person premiums: all adults with the same insurer, in the same model and in the same region pay the same, no matter how much they earn.
126301.m: Health insurance premiums are per-person premiums and do not depend on salary.

126302.q: Which law governs supplementary insurance, where insurers may ask health questions and reject applications?
126302.e: Supplementary insurance, such as a semi-private hospital ward, consists of private law contracts under the Insurance Contract Act. There is no obligation to accept there.
126302.m: Supplementary insurance is voluntary and may reject applications.

126303.q: What does the billing system “tiers garant” mean?
a: The patient pays the bill and gets the money back from the insurer
The insurer pays the bill directly to the doctor
The canton of residence pays the whole bill
The employer pays the bill and deducts it from the salary
126303.e: In the tiers garant system, the insured person owes the bill and then has it refunded by the insurer.
126303.m: In the tiers garant system, you pay first yourself and are then reimbursed.

126304.q: Who can exclude accident cover from basic insurance and so save on premiums?
a: Employees who work at least 8 hours a week for the same employer
126304.e: Anyone who works at least 8 hours a week for the same employer is also insured against non-occupational accidents under the Accident Insurance Act. Double cover is then unnecessary.
126304.m: Anyone insured against accidents through their employer can suspend the accident cover of their health insurance.

126305.q: Which service does basic insurance usually not pay for?
a: Ordinary dental treatment such as fillings
A stay in the general ward of a hospital
Medicines prescribed by a doctor and covered by insurance
126305.e: Basic insurance only pays for dental treatment in exceptional cases, for example when it is caused by a serious illness. Normal dental care must be paid for yourself or through supplementary insurance.
126305.m: Basic insurance does not pay for normal dental treatment.

126306.q: What is the standard annual deductible for adults in basic insurance?
126306.e: The standard, which means the lowest, deductible for adults is 300 francs a year. You can choose higher deductibles voluntarily.
126306.m: The lowest deductible for adults is 300 francs.

126307.q: What is the highest deductible adults can choose in basic insurance?
126307.e: Adults can choose between 300, 500, 1,000, 1,500, 2,000 and 2,500 francs. The highest level brings the biggest premium discount.
126307.m: The highest deductible for adults is 2,500 francs.

126308.q: What is the standard deductible for children up to the age of 18?
126308.e: By law there is no standard deductible for children. However, parents can choose an optional deductible voluntarily.
126308.m: Unless one is chosen, children have no deductible.

126309.q: What is the highest optional deductible for children?
126309.e: For children you can choose optional deductibles in steps of a hundred, from 100 to 600 francs.
126309.m: For children, a deductible of up to 600 francs is possible.

126310.q: How does choosing a higher deductible affect the monthly premium?
a: The premium is set again by the canton
126310.e: Anyone who pays more of the costs themselves takes pressure off the insurer. In return, it gives a discount on the premium.
126310.m: A higher deductible lowers the premium but increases your own risk.

126311.q: A person has a deductible of 2,500 francs and doctor's costs of 1,800 francs for the whole year. How much does basic insurance pay?
126311.e: The costs of 1,800 francs are below the deductible of 2,500 francs. The person therefore pays everything themselves and the insurance pays nothing.
126311.m: Until the deductible is reached, you pay everything yourself.

126312.q: For what period does the deductible apply?
a: For each individual visit to the doctor
For one quarter of a year
126312.e: The deductible is calculated per calendar year. On 1 January it starts again at zero.
126312.m: The deductible starts again every year on 1 January.

126313.q: Which deductible levels apply to young adults aged 19 to 25?
a: Their own levels between 50 and 500 francs
126313.e: Young adults often pay lower premiums than older adults but have the same deductible levels of 300 to 2,500 francs.
126313.m: From the age of 19, the adult deductibles apply.

126314.q: For whom is a high deductible typically worth it?
a: For healthy people with low health costs
For people with a chronic illness
For people with expensive long-term medicines
For people who are often in hospital
126314.e: People who rarely go to the doctor benefit from the premium discount and hardly ever use up the high deductible. With high costs, however, you end up paying more.
126314.m: A high deductible is mainly worth it for healthy people.

126315.q: What percentage of the costs above the deductible do insured people usually pay as their share?
126315.e: Once the deductible has been reached, you pay 10 per cent of the further costs, up to an annual maximum.
126315.m: The normal co-payment is ten per cent.

126316.q: What is the maximum annual co-payment for adults?
126316.e: For adults, the 10 per cent co-payment is limited to 700 francs a year.
126316.m: Adults pay at most 700 francs co-payment per year.

126317.q: What is the maximum annual co-payment for children?
126317.e: For children, the co-payment is limited to half the amount for adults, which is 350 francs a year.
126317.m: For children, the co-payment is limited to 350 francs.

126318.q: Deductible 300 francs, treatment costs for the year 1,500 francs. How much does the insured person pay themselves in total?
126318.e: First comes the 300 francs deductible. Of the remaining 1,200 francs, you pay 10 per cent, which is 120 francs. Together that makes 420 francs.
126318.m: First comes the deductible, then the co-payment on the rest.

126319.q: Deductible 300 francs, treatment costs for the year 20,000 francs. How much does an adult pay themselves in total?
126319.e: 300 francs deductible plus 10 per cent of 19,700 francs would be 1,970 francs co-payment. But this is limited to 700 francs, so the total is 300 + 700 = 1,000 francs.
126319.m: The upper limit on the co-payment protects against very high costs.

126320.q: Deductible 1,000 francs, treatment costs for the year 3,000 francs. How much does the adult pay themselves?
126320.e: 1,000 francs deductible plus 10 per cent of the remaining 2,000 francs, which is 200 francs. Total 1,200 francs.
126320.m: You calculate the deductible plus ten per cent of the remaining costs.

126321.q: What is the maximum annual cost share for an adult with a deductible of 2,500 francs (deductible plus co-payment)?
126321.e: On top of the 2,500 francs deductible comes a co-payment of at most 700 francs. That makes 3,200 francs.
126321.m: With the highest deductible, in the worst case you pay 3,200 francs yourself.

126322.q: Since 2024, which co-payment usually applies if you get an original medicine even though a cheaper generic is available?
126322.e: To encourage the use of cheaper generics, the increased co-payment for overpriced original medicines was raised to 40 per cent. There are exceptions if the original is medically necessary.
126322.m: Anyone who chooses the expensive original without a medical reason pays more themselves.

126323.q: Which contribution do adults pay for a hospital stay in addition to the deductible and co-payment?
126323.e: The hospital contribution takes into account the food costs saved at home. Children and young adults in education are exempt from it.
126323.m: For every day in hospital, adults pay a small contribution towards their meals.

126324.q: What does the abbreviation IPV stand for in the Swiss health system?
126324.e: With the individual premium reduction, the state supports insured people of modest means.
126324.m: The IPV helps people on low incomes to pay their premiums.

126325.q: Who finances the individual premium reduction?
126325.e: The Confederation makes a contribution to the cantons, and the cantons add their own funds.
126325.m: The Confederation and the cantons pay for the premium reduction together.

126326.q: Who decides who is entitled to a premium reduction and how much it is?
a: The Federal Council, the same for everyone
126326.e: The cantons set the income limits and amounts themselves. That is why the rules differ greatly from canton to canton.
126326.m: Each canton regulates the premium reduction itself.

126327.q: For which groups does the Health Insurance Act require a particularly large premium reduction?
a: Children and young adults in education
126327.e: For lower and middle incomes, the cantons must reduce the premiums for children and young adults in education particularly strongly. This is to ease the burden on families.
126327.m: Families on low and middle incomes receive a large premium reduction for their children.

126328.q: How is the premium reduction usually paid out?
a: In cash at the municipal office counter
As a bonus on top of the salary
As a credit at the doctor's
126328.e: The canton transfers the amount directly to the health insurer. The insured person then pays a lower premium bill.
126328.m: The premium reduction directly lowers the premium bill.

126329.q: Which popular initiative, which wanted to limit premiums to at most 10 per cent of disposable income, did voters reject in 2024?
a: The initiative for a single health insurance fund
126329.e: The Premium Relief Initiative was rejected in June 2024. Instead, an indirect counter-proposal comes into force that obliges the cantons to make minimum contributions.
126329.m: Limiting premiums to ten per cent of income was rejected in 2024.

126330.q: What does the size of the federal contribution to the premium reduction depend on?
a: The tax rate of the municipalities
126330.e: The Confederation pays a fixed share of the gross costs of compulsory health insurance. If health costs rise, its contribution rises too.
126330.m: The federal contribution to the premium reduction grows with health costs.

126331.q: What does the Federal Office of Public Health check before basic insurance pays for a new medicine?
a: Whether it is effective, appropriate and cost-effective
Whether it is made in Switzerland
Whether it is available without a prescription
126331.e: A medicine is only added to the list of pharmaceutical specialities if it is effective, appropriate and cost-effective. Only then does basic insurance pay.
126331.m: Basic insurance only pays for effective, appropriate and cost-effective medicines.

126332.q: What must the Federal Office of Public Health approve every year before it applies?
a: The hospital bills of the cantons
126332.e: The health insurers submit their premiums for the following year to the Federal Office of Public Health. It checks them and announces the approved premiums every autumn.
126332.m: The new health insurance premiums are approved by the Federal Office of Public Health every autumn.

126333.q: Which law regulates, among other things, the duty to report certain infectious diseases?
126333.e: The Epidemics Act regulates protection against infectious diseases. Doctors and laboratories report certain diseases to the Federal Office of Public Health and the canton.
126333.m: Infectious diseases are reported and monitored under the Epidemics Act.

126334.q: In which region does the Federal Office of Public Health have its headquarters?
126334.e: The Federal Office of Public Health is based in Liebefeld near Bern, close to the rest of the federal administration.
126334.m: The Federal Office of Public Health is based near Bern.

126335.q: Which task also belongs to the Federal Office of Public Health?
a: Radiation protection, for example from radon in buildings
126335.e: The Federal Office of Public Health is responsible for radiation protection in Switzerland. This includes information about the radioactive gas radon, which can occur in cellars and living spaces.
126335.m: Protection from radiation such as radon is also a task of the Federal Office of Public Health.

126336.q: What is the official federal premium calculator called, which lets you compare health insurance premiums?
126336.e: On Priminfo, the Federal Office of Public Health publishes all approved basic insurance premiums. This lets you compare offers neutrally.
126336.m: With Priminfo you can compare the premiums of all health insurers.

126337.q: Which insurance is compulsory for all residents of Switzerland?
a: Supplementary insurance for a private room
126337.e: Basic insurance under the Health Insurance Act is compulsory for everyone living in Switzerland. Supplementary insurance is voluntary.
126337.m: Basic insurance is compulsory in Switzerland.

126338.q: What is the main task of Swissmedic?
126338.e: Swissmedic is the Swiss authority that approves and supervises medicines and medical devices. It checks safety, effectiveness and quality.
126338.m: Swissmedic approves and monitors therapeutic products.

126339.q: Why does a new medicine need approval before it may be sold in Switzerland?
a: Its safety, effectiveness and quality must be checked
So that the price is as high as possible
So that it may be advertised
So that it is only used in hospitals
126339.e: Before approval, Swissmedic examines the manufacturer's studies. Only if the benefits outweigh the risks may the medicine be sold.
126339.m: Medicines need approval before they are sold.

126340.q: Which law is Swissmedic's work mainly based on?
126340.e: The Therapeutic Products Act regulates the approval, manufacture, supply and monitoring of medicines and medical devices.
126340.m: Swissmedic works on the basis of the Therapeutic Products Act.

126341.q: What is meant by pharmacovigilance, one of Swissmedic's tasks?
a: Monitoring undesirable effects of medicines after approval
126341.e: Rare side effects can still occur after approval. Professionals and patients report suspected cases, and Swissmedic evaluates them.
126341.m: Even approved medicines continue to be monitored for side effects.

126342.q: Which task is not one of Swissmedic's?
a: Setting the prices of medicines covered by health insurance
126342.e: Swissmedic checks safety, effectiveness and quality. The price and whether insurance pays are decided by the Federal Office of Public Health instead.
126342.m: Swissmedic checks the safety of a medicine, not its price.

126343.q: What does dispensing category E mean for medicines?
a: Freely available for sale, even outside pharmacies
Can be supplied only once on a doctor's prescription
Only after expert advice in a pharmacy
Can only be used in hospital
126343.e: Medicines in category E, such as certain throat lozenges, may be sold in shops without expert advice.
126343.m: Medicines in category E are freely available.

126344.q: What does Swissmedic regularly warn about when medicines are ordered from unknown online shops abroad?
a: Delivery times that are too long
126344.e: Many medicines ordered online are fakes with the wrong dose or dangerous ingredients. Customs often stop such parcels.
126344.m: Medicines from dubious online shops can be fake and dangerous.

126345.q: How many university hospitals are there in Switzerland?
126345.e: The five university hospitals are in Zurich, Bern, Basel, Lausanne and Geneva.

126346.q: Which university does the CHUV work with in medical teaching and research?
126346.e: The Faculty of Biology and Medicine of the University of Lausanne trains its medical students together with the CHUV.
126346.m: Every university hospital works closely with a medical faculty.

126347.q: In which city is the CHUV university hospital?
126347.e: CHUV stands for Centre hospitalier universitaire vaudois. It is the university hospital of the canton of Vaud in Lausanne.
126347.m: The CHUV is the university hospital in Lausanne.

126348.q: In which city are the HUG (Hôpitaux universitaires de Genève)?
126348.e: The HUG are the university hospital of the canton of Geneva and one of the largest hospital groups in Switzerland.
126348.m: The HUG are the university hospital of Geneva.

126349.q: What are the three main tasks of university hospitals?
126349.e: University hospitals treat patients, train doctors together with the universities and carry out medical research.
126349.m: University hospitals combine treatment, training and research.

126350.q: Why are very complex operations such as organ transplants concentrated in a few centres in Switzerland?
a: Because high case numbers ensure experience and quality
Because small hospitals have no doctors
Because the Confederation wants to close all other hospitals
Because only university hospitals have electricity
126350.e: The cantons coordinate highly specialised medicine together. Those who perform an operation often have more routine, and expensive infrastructure is not built several times over.
126350.m: Rare, complex operations are concentrated in a few experienced centres.

126351.q: Who runs the University Hospital Zurich?
126351.e: The University Hospital Zurich is an independent public institution of the canton of Zurich. For teaching, it works with the University of Zurich.
126351.m: In Switzerland, university hospitals belong to the cantons.

126352.q: Which of these hospitals is not a university hospital?
126352.e: St Gallen Cantonal Hospital is a large central hospital and does train doctors, but it is not one of the five university hospitals.
126352.m: Not every large hospital is a university hospital.

126353.q: What is the guiding role that the GP takes on in the family doctor model called?
126353.e: In gatekeeping, the GP decides whether and where a patient is referred. This is meant to avoid unnecessary duplicate examinations.
126353.m: In the family doctor model, the GP is the guide through the health system.

126354.q: In which alternative insurance model do you first have to call a telephone advice service before seeing a doctor?
126354.e: In the Telmed model, a medical professional clarifies over the phone whether and where treatment is needed.
126354.m: In the Telmed model, you first call the advice service.

126355.q: In which model do you first go to a health centre with doctors employed there?
126355.e: HMO stands for Health Maintenance Organization. The first treatment takes place in a particular group practice.
126355.m: In the HMO model, a group practice is the first point of contact.

126356.q: What advantage do insured people get if they choose the family doctor model?
126356.e: Because coordinated treatment is usually cheaper, insurers offer a lower premium than in the standard model.
126356.m: People insured in the family doctor model pay a lower premium.

126357.q: In the family doctor model, in which situation may you go straight to another place without first contacting your GP?
a: If you personally know a specialist
126357.e: In an emergency, quick treatment comes first. However, you usually have to inform your GP or the insurer afterwards.
126357.m: In an emergency you may get help straight away, even in the family doctor model.

126358.q: What can happen in the family doctor model if you go straight to a specialist without a referral?
a: The insurer can refuse to pay the costs
126358.e: Anyone who repeatedly breaks the model's rules risks the insurer not paying the bill or moving them back into the more expensive standard model.
126358.m: Anyone who ignores the rules of the family doctor model may be left with the costs.

126359.q: Which proposal to promote integrated care networks did voters clearly reject in 2012?
126359.e: The revision of the Health Insurance Act on managed care aimed to promote care networks with a lower co-payment. It was clearly defeated at the ballot box in June 2012.
126359.m: The managed care bill was rejected at the ballot box in 2012.

126360.q: What did the people and the cantons add to the Federal Constitution in 2014 that strengthens family medicine?
a: An article on basic medical care
A ban on alternative insurance models
A duty to have an annual health check
126360.e: The federal decree on basic medical care obliges the Confederation and the cantons to promote good basic care, including family medicine.
126360.m: Since 2014, basic medical care has been in the Federal Constitution.

126361.q: Which services did the Tarmed tariff apply to?
126361.e: Tarmed set out how doctors' practices and hospital outpatient departments charge for their outpatient services.
126361.m: Tarmed was the tariff for outpatient medical services.

126362.q: Why was the Tarmed doctors' tariff replaced by a new tariff?
a: It was considered outdated and many services were wrongly valued
Visits to the doctor became free
126362.e: Tarmed dated from the 1990s and no longer reflected modern medicine properly. From 2026 it was replaced by TARDOC and outpatient flat rates.
126362.m: Tarmed was replaced because of outdated valuations.

126363.q: A service is valued at 40 tax points and the tax point value is 0.95 francs. How much does the service cost?
126363.e: You multiply the tax points by the tax point value: 40 times 0.95 francs makes 38 francs.
126363.m: The price of a service is the tax points times the tax point value.

126364.q: What is true of the tax point value in Tarmed?
a: It varies by canton and contract
It is the same throughout Switzerland
126364.e: The number of tax points is the same across Switzerland, but the tax point value is agreed regionally between the tariff partners. That is why the same service does not cost the same everywhere.
126364.m: The tax point value differs between cantons.

126365.q: Which new doctors' tariff replaced Tarmed from 2026, together with outpatient flat rates?
126365.e: Tarmed was considered outdated. The Federal Council therefore approved TARDOC and outpatient flat rates as its successors.
126365.m: Since 2026, TARDOC and outpatient flat rates have replaced the old Tarmed.

126366.q: Which tariff system applies to stays in acute care in hospitals?
a: SwissDRG with flat rates per case
126366.e: Since 2012, acute hospital stays have been charged with flat rates per case. For each case of treatment there is a fixed amount depending on the diagnosis.
126366.m: Hospital stays are charged with flat rates per case under SwissDRG.

126367.q: Who mainly negotiates doctors' tariffs such as Tarmed?
a: The tariff partners, meaning healthcare providers and insurers
126367.e: Tariffs are agreed by associations of doctors, hospitals and insurers. Only if they cannot agree can the Federal Council step in.
126367.m: Doctors' tariffs are negotiated by the tariff partners.

126368.q: What kind of tariff was Tarmed?
126368.e: With Tarmed, every single service, such as a five-minute consultation or an examination, was charged separately with tax points.
126368.m: With Tarmed, every medical service was charged individually.

126369.q: In which year did the people and the cantons accept the nursing care initiative?
126369.e: The nursing care initiative was accepted on 28 November 2021. It was one of the few popular initiatives to succeed at the ballot box.
126369.m: The nursing care initiative was accepted in 2021.

126370.q: What is the official title of the nursing care initiative?
126370.e: The federal popular initiative “For strong nursing care” is called the nursing care initiative for short.
126370.m: The nursing care initiative is officially called “For strong nursing care”.

126371.q: Who launched the nursing care initiative?
a: The professional association of nurses SBK
126371.e: The Swiss Professional Association of Nurses (SBK) launched the initiative in 2017.
126371.m: The professional association of nurses was behind the nursing care initiative.

126372.q: Roughly what share of yes votes was the nursing care initiative accepted with?
126372.e: Just over 61 per cent of voters and a clear majority of the cantons said yes.
126372.m: The nursing care initiative was clearly accepted.

126373.q: What is at the centre of the first stage of putting the nursing care initiative into practice?
a: A single insurance fund for nursing care
126373.e: For several years, the Confederation and the cantons are promoting nursing training, for example with contributions to students and training establishments.
126373.m: With the nursing care initiative, training is strengthened first.

126374.q: What are nurses newly allowed to do thanks to the implementation of the nursing care initiative?
a: Bill certain nursing services directly without a doctor's prescription
Carry out operations on their own
Set up their own health insurers
126374.e: Nurses can provide certain services, such as assessing care needs, directly at the expense of basic insurance. This strengthens their independence.
126374.m: Nurses gain more independence in billing.

126375.q: Which problem did the nursing care initiative mainly want to tackle?
a: The shortage of nurses and people leaving the profession early
Wages in nursing that are too high
Too many hospitals in the cities
Deductibles for insured people that are too low
126375.e: Many nurses leave the profession early, while demand is rising because of the ageing population. The initiative calls for more training and better working conditions.
126375.m: The nursing care initiative is meant to ensure there are enough nursing staff.

126376.q: Who does the new constitutional article on nursing care oblige to ensure there are enough qualified nurses?
126376.e: The constitutional article requires the Confederation and the cantons to promote sufficient high-quality nursing care that is accessible to everyone.
126376.m: The Confederation and the cantons are jointly responsible for enough nursing staff.

126377.q: In which year did the Federal Act on the Electronic Patient Record (EPDG) come into force?
126377.e: The EPDG came into force in April 2017. After that, the providers of the record first had to be certified.
126377.m: The law on the electronic patient record has applied since 2017.

126378.q: Under the law so far, what applies to patients regarding the electronic patient record?
a: Opening one is compulsory from the age of 18
Every health insurer opens one automatically
It is only allowed for hospital patients
126378.e: For the population, the electronic patient record has been voluntary so far. In the current revision of the law, it is being discussed whether it will be opened automatically for everyone in future.
126378.m: So far, opening an electronic patient record is voluntary.

126379.q: Who decides which health professionals may see documents in the electronic patient record?
a: The Federal Office of Public Health
126379.e: The holder of the record grants access rights themselves and can change them at any time.
126379.m: In the electronic patient record, the patient decides who may see what.

126380.q: Which healthcare providers have had to join an electronic patient record community since 2020?
126380.e: Hospitals had to take part first, followed later by care homes and newly licensed doctors' practices.
126380.m: Hospitals were the first that had to take part in the electronic patient record.

126381.q: Who has no access to the electronic patient record?
126381.e: The law explicitly excludes insurers and employers from access. This is to keep health data protected.
126381.m: Health insurers may not look into the electronic patient record.

126382.q: With what kind of organisation do you open an electronic patient record?
126382.e: Providers of the electronic patient record are called core communities. They are certified and manage the records and access rights.
126382.m: You get an electronic patient record from a certified core community.

126383.q: What role does eHealth Suisse play in the electronic patient record?
a: It is the coordination office of the Confederation and the cantons
It is a private health insurer
126383.e: eHealth Suisse coordinates the introduction of the electronic patient record, prepares the groundwork and informs the public.
126383.m: eHealth Suisse coordinates digital health for the Confederation and the cantons.

126384.q: Which document typically belongs in an electronic patient record?
a: A discharge report after a hospital stay
126384.e: Information relevant to treatment is stored in the electronic patient record, for example discharge reports, medication plans or vaccination details.
126384.m: Important health documents such as discharge reports belong in the electronic patient record.

126385.q: Who draws up the hospital lists that set out which hospitals may treat patients at the expense of basic insurance?
126385.e: Hospital planning is the task of the cantons. Only hospitals on the cantonal hospital list can bill inpatient services to basic insurance.
126385.m: With the hospital list, the cantons decide which hospitals are approved.

126386.q: For inpatient hospital treatment in Switzerland today, who pays the larger share of the costs?
126386.e: Under dual fixed financing, the canton pays at least 55 per cent of the inpatient costs and the health insurer at most 45 per cent.
126386.m: For inpatient treatment, the canton pays the larger share.

126387.q: Which reform accepted at the ballot box in 2024 is meant to finance outpatient and inpatient services by the same formula in future?
126387.e: With uniform financing of outpatient and inpatient services (EFAS), cantons and insurers will in future pay everywhere according to the same distribution formula. This is meant to remove false incentives in favour of expensive inpatient treatment.
126387.m: In future, EFAS will finance outpatient and inpatient services in the same way.

126388.q: Since 2012, what applies to people with basic insurance when choosing a hospital for planned treatment?
a: They can choose a listed hospital anywhere in Switzerland
They may only go to a hospital in their canton of residence
The health insurer chooses the hospital
The GP decides the hospital bindingly
126388.e: Since 2012, there has been free choice among listed hospitals. However, at most the tariff that applies in the canton of residence is paid.
126388.m: Since 2012, you may choose a listed hospital anywhere in Switzerland for treatment.

126390.q: In which town is the Grisons Cantonal Hospital?
126390.e: The Grisons Cantonal Hospital in Chur is the central hospital for the whole canton.
126390.m: The central hospital of the Grisons is in Chur.

126391.q: What legal form do, for example, the cantonal hospitals of Aarau and Baden have?
a: A limited company owned by the canton
126391.e: Many cantons have separated their hospitals from the administration. In Aargau, the cantonal hospitals are limited companies whose shares are held by the canton.
126391.m: Many cantonal hospitals are now independent companies owned by the canton.

126392.q: Which double role of the cantons in the hospital system is often criticised?
a: They own hospitals and are at the same time planners and supervisors
They are health insurers and patients at the same time
They make medicines and approve them
They train doctors and pay their premiums
126392.e: Cantons often own their hospitals but at the same time draw up the hospital lists and approve tariffs. Critics see conflicts of interest in this.
126392.m: In the hospital system, cantons are owners and regulators at the same time.

126393.q: Which number do you dial in Switzerland for the ambulance emergency line when an ambulance needs to go to hospital?
126393.e: 144 is the number for the ambulance emergency line. 117 is the police, 118 the fire brigade and 143 the helpline Dargebotene Hand.
126393.m: In Switzerland you dial 144 for an ambulance.

126394.q: In which municipality in Geneva is CERN’s main site?
126394.e: CERN’s main site is in Meyrin near Geneva, right on the border with France. CERN’s facilities also extend into French territory.
126394.m: CERN’s headquarters are in Meyrin near Geneva.

126395.q: Which long-sought particle was detected in 2012 at CERN’s LHC particle accelerator?
126395.e: The ATLAS and CMS experiments found the Higgs boson in 2012. It confirms the mechanism by which elementary particles get their mass. Peter Higgs and François Englert received the Nobel Prize in 2013.
126395.m: The Higgs boson was discovered at CERN in 2012.

126396.q: Which invention, created at CERN in 1989, is used today by almost everyone every day?
126396.e: In 1989 at CERN, Tim Berners-Lee proposed a system with which researchers could link documents through links. This became the World Wide Web.
126396.m: The World Wide Web was invented at CERN.

126397.q: Which wooden sphere-shaped building near CERN did the Swiss Confederation give CERN for its 50th anniversary?
a: The Globe of Science and Innovation
126397.e: The wooden globe originally stood at Expo.02 and was then rebuilt at CERN. It is used for exhibitions and events.
126397.m: The wooden globe at CERN is a gift from Switzerland.

126398.q: Which architect designed the Science Gateway visitor centre at CERN, opened in 2023?
126398.e: The Science Gateway by the Italian architect Renzo Piano offers exhibitions, laboratories and event spaces for visitors and school classes.
126398.m: The Science Gateway at CERN is by the architect Renzo Piano.

126399.q: What does the CERN Convention lay down about military research?
a: CERN does no research for military purposes
CERN mainly does research for NATO
Military projects are only allowed for member states
Military research is secret but allowed
126399.e: The Convention requires that CERN does not concern itself with work for military purposes and publishes its results.
126399.m: CERN carries out pure basic research without military goals.

126400.q: Roughly how long is the circumference of the Large Hadron Collider?
126400.e: The LHC’s ring tunnel is about 26.7 kilometres long and runs under Switzerland and France.
126400.m: The LHC ring is about 27 kilometres long.

126401.q: Roughly at what depth does the LHC tunnel run?
126401.e: Depending on the spot, the tunnel lies between about 50 and 175 metres deep. The rock also shields radiation.
126401.m: The LHC lies on average about 100 metres underground.

126402.q: Apart from protons, which particles are also made to collide in the LHC?
126402.e: In special running periods, heavy ions such as lead nuclei are accelerated. Their collisions produce extremely hot, dense matter.
126402.m: In the LHC, protons and also heavy ions such as lead collide.

126403.q: Which accelerator ran in the same tunnel before the LHC?
126403.e: In LEP, electrons and positrons collided from 1989 to 2000. Then the tunnel was converted for the LHC.
126403.m: The LHC uses the tunnel of its predecessor LEP.

126404.q: In which year did a particle beam first circle in the LHC?
126404.e: In September 2008, the first beam was sent around the ring. A few days later, operation had to be stopped for over a year after a breakdown.

126405.q: What caused the breakdown in the LHC in September 2008?
a: A faulty electrical connection between magnets
An earthquake in the Geneva region
A hacker attack on the controls
A power cut in the whole city of Geneva
126405.e: A bad soldered connection between superconducting magnets overheated. Helium escaped and damaged many magnets.
126405.m: A single faulty connection shut down the LHC for a long time in 2008.

126406.q: Which long-sought particle was detected at the LHC in 2012?
126406.e: The ATLAS and CMS experiments announced the detection of the Higgs boson in July 2012. It explains how elementary particles get their mass.
126406.m: The Higgs boson was discovered at the LHC in 2012.

126407.q: What is the aim of the upgrade to the High-Luminosity LHC?
a: Many more collisions per unit of time
Operation without cooling at room temperature
126407.e: Higher luminosity means more collisions and therefore more data. This allows even very rare processes to be studied more precisely.
126407.m: The High-Luminosity LHC is meant to deliver many more collisions and data.

126408.q: How fast do the protons in the LHC move at full energy?
a: At over 99.9999 per cent of the speed of light
At about half the speed of light
At about 10 per cent of the speed of light
At about the speed of sound
126408.e: At energies in the TeV range, a proton’s total energy is thousands of times greater than its rest energy. Its speed is therefore extremely close to the speed of light, but never reaches it.
126408.m: In the LHC, the protons fly at almost the speed of light.

126409.q: Which fundamental force does the Standard Model of particle physics not describe?
126409.e: The Standard Model unites three of the four fundamental forces. Gravity is described by general relativity and has not yet been included in a quantum theory.
126409.m: Gravity is missing from the Standard Model.

126410.q: How many elementary matter particles (fermions, not counting antiparticles) does the Standard Model know?
126410.e: The Standard Model counts 12 elementary fermions. Each one also has an antiparticle.
126410.m: The Standard Model knows twelve elementary matter particles.

126411.q: Which particle carries the strong interaction?
126411.e: Gluons hold the quarks together in protons and neutrons. The name comes from the English word “glue”.
126411.m: Gluons glue the quarks together with the strong force.

126412.q: Which particle carries the electromagnetic interaction?
126412.e: Electrically charged particles interact by exchanging photons, the quanta of light.
126412.m: The photon carries the electromagnetic force.

126413.q: Which interaction do the W and Z bosons carry?
126413.e: The weak interaction is responsible, for example, for beta decay. Its exchange particles are very heavy, which is why it has an extremely short range.
126413.m: W and Z bosons carry the weak force.

126414.q: What did Glashow, Salam and Weinberg receive the Nobel Prize in Physics for in 1979?
a: For unifying the electromagnetic and weak interactions
126414.e: Their theory of the electroweak interaction describes two fundamental forces as forms of one common force.
126414.m: The electroweak theory unites two fundamental forces.

126415.q: What is the theory in the Standard Model that describes the strong interaction called?
126415.e: The name refers to “colour” (Greek chroma), a charge of the strong force.
126415.m: The strong force is described by quantum chromodynamics.

126416.q: To which group of particles do the force particles photon and gluon belong?
126416.e: Particles that carry forces have whole-number spin and are bosons. Matter particles such as electrons and quarks are fermions.

126417.q: How many kinds (flavours) of quarks are there in the Standard Model?
126417.e: The quarks are called up, down, charm, strange, top and bottom.
126417.m: There are six different kinds of quark.

126418.q: Which is the heaviest known quark?
126418.e: The top quark is about as heavy as a whole gold atom. It decays so quickly that it does not form bound particles.
126418.m: The top quark is the heaviest elementary particle.

126419.q: Where was the top quark discovered in 1995?
126419.e: The top quark was detected at Fermilab’s Tevatron accelerator near Chicago.
126419.m: The top quark was discovered at Fermilab in 1995.

126420.q: Which quarks make up a neutron?
a: Two down quarks and one up quark
Two up quarks and one down quark
One up, one down and one strange quark
126420.e: The neutron has the composition udd. The charges +2/3, −1/3 and −1/3 add up to zero.
126420.m: A neutron consists of one up quark and two down quarks.

126421.q: The delta particle Δ++ consists of three up quarks, each with +2/3 elementary charge. What charge does it have?
126421.e: You add the three charges: 3 times 2/3 gives 2. So the particle has the charge +2 e.
126421.m: The charge of a hadron is the sum of the quark charges.

a: Quarks never occur freely on their own
Quarks cannot move in atomic nuclei
Quarks can only exist in the laboratory
126422.e: The further apart quarks are pulled, the stronger the force between them becomes. Instead of single quarks, new quark-antiquark pairs are produced.
126422.m: Quarks always stay locked inside particles such as protons.

126423.q: From which literary work did Murray Gell-Mann borrow the word “quark”?
a: From “Alice in Wonderland” by Lewis Carroll
126423.e: “Finnegans Wake” contains the line “Three quarks for Muster Mark!”. The number three matched the three quarks in protons and neutrons.
126423.m: The name quark comes from a novel by James Joyce.

126424.q: What does a meson consist of?
126424.e: Mesons such as the pion consist of a quark-antiquark pair. Particles made of three quarks, by contrast, are called baryons.
126424.m: A meson consists of a quark and an antiquark.

126425.q: Which property of quarks is labelled with the names red, green and blue?
126425.e: Colour charge is the charge of the strong force. It has nothing to do with real colours; the names are just an image.
126425.m: Quarks carry a colour charge that has nothing to do with real colours.

126426.q: Which of these particles is a lepton?
126426.e: Leptons are elementary particles without quarks: the electron, muon, tau and the three neutrinos. The proton, pion and neutron are made of quarks.
126426.m: The muon is a heavy relative of the electron and a lepton.

126427.q: Which interaction do leptons not take part in?
a: None, they take part in all of them
126427.e: Leptons carry no colour charge and therefore do not feel the strong force. Charged leptons also interact electromagnetically.
126427.m: Leptons do not feel the strong force.

126428.q: Roughly how much heavier than an electron is a muon?
126428.e: The muon has about 207 times the mass of the electron but is otherwise very similar. It is unstable and decays after about two microseconds.
126428.m: The muon is about two hundred times heavier than the electron.

126429.q: Which charged lepton was the last to be discovered, in the mid-1970s?
126429.e: The tau was discovered in 1975 at SLAC in California by Martin Perl and his team. It is the heaviest charged lepton.
126429.m: The tau is the heaviest and most recently discovered charged lepton.

126430.q: What does the Greek word from which the term “lepton” comes mean?
126430.e: The word “leptos” means light or fine. The electron, as the first lepton, was much lighter than protons.

126431.q: Why do many muons from cosmic rays reach the ground even though they are very short-lived?
a: Because of time dilation at almost the speed of light
Because they are attracted by the Earth and speed up
Because they are newly formed near the ground
Because the atmosphere lengthens their lifetime
126431.e: For us, time passes more slowly in the fast muons. That is why they travel much longer distances than their lifetime at rest would allow.
126431.m: Muons from space demonstrate the time dilation of relativity.

126432.q: Where was the muon discovered in 1936?
a: In a particle accelerator at CERN
126432.e: Carl D. Anderson and Seth Neddermeyer found the muon in tracks of particles from cosmic rays. Accelerators of this power did not yet exist at the time.
126432.m: The muon was discovered in cosmic rays.

126433.q: Which quantity is conserved in all particle reactions observed so far, for example in the beta decay of a neutron?
a: The total mass of the particles
126433.e: In beta decay, an electron antineutrino is produced alongside the electron. The electron (+1) and antineutrino (−1) together give the lepton number zero, as before.
126433.m: In particle reactions, the lepton number is conserved.

126434.q: In which year did CERN announce the discovery of a Higgs boson?
126434.e: On 4 July 2012, the discovery of a new particle was presented that matches the long-sought Higgs boson.
126434.m: The Higgs boson was discovered in 2012.

126435.q: Roughly what mass does the Higgs boson have?
126435.e: At about 125 GeV, the Higgs boson is about 130 times as heavy as a proton.
126435.m: The Higgs boson has a mass of about 125 GeV.

126436.q: Who received the 2013 Nobel Prize in Physics for the theoretical prediction of the Higgs mechanism?
126436.e: Englert had published the idea in 1964 together with Robert Brout, and Higgs almost at the same time. Brout had died in 2011 and could no longer receive the prize.
126436.m: Higgs and Englert received the Nobel Prize for the Higgs mechanism.

126437.q: Why can’t a Higgs boson be seen directly in the detector?
a: It decays almost immediately into other particles
It is only produced outside the detector
126437.e: A Higgs boson only exists for a tiny fraction of a second. It is recognised by the particles it decays into, for example two photons.
126437.m: The Higgs boson is detected through its decay products.

126438.q: Which two LHC experiments jointly detected the Higgs boson?
126438.e: Two independent experiments with different detectors found the particle. That made the discovery particularly convincing.
126438.m: Two independent detectors confirmed the Higgs boson.

126439.q: What role does the Higgs field play in the Standard Model?
a: It gives elementary particles such as W bosons and quarks their mass
It determines the electric charge of particles
126439.e: Particles that interact strongly with the Higgs field are heavy, others are light. Photons do not interact with it and remain massless.
126439.m: Elementary particles get their mass from the Higgs field.

126440.q: Where does most of a proton’s mass come from?
a: From the binding energy of the strong interaction
From the quark masses produced by the Higgs field
From the electrons in the proton
126440.e: The three quarks make up only about one per cent of the proton’s mass. According to E = mc², the rest lies in the energy of the gluons and the motion of the quarks.
126440.m: The proton’s mass comes mainly from binding energy.

126441.q: Which decay of the Higgs boson was one of the most important discovery channels in 2012?
a: The decay into a single photon
The decay into a proton and an electron
The decay into a single neutrino
126441.e: Two high-energy photons can be measured very precisely in the detector. An excess at a certain mass revealed the new particle.
126441.m: The Higgs boson showed up, among other things, through decays into two photons.

126442.q: Which physicist predicted the existence of the positron with his relativistic equation for the electron?
126442.e: The Dirac equation of 1928 gave solutions that were interpreted as particles with positive charge and the electron’s mass.

126443.q: Who detected the positron in cosmic rays in 1932?
126443.e: In a cloud chamber inside a magnetic field, Anderson observed tracks that looked like electrons but curved in the opposite direction.
126443.m: The positron was discovered by Carl D. Anderson in 1932.

126444.q: What usually happens when an electron and a positron meet?
a: They combine to form a proton
126444.e: In annihilation, the entire mass is converted into radiation energy. Usually two gamma photons of 511 keV each are produced.
126444.m: Matter and antimatter annihilate each other into radiation.

126445.q: Where were antihydrogen atoms first produced in 1995?
126445.e: The first few antihydrogen atoms were produced in 1995 at CERN’s LEAR storage ring. Today CERN studies antimatter with the Antiproton Decelerator.
126445.m: The first anti-atoms were produced at CERN in 1995.

126446.q: Which medical imaging method uses positrons?
126446.e: In PET, the patient is given a weakly radioactive substance that emits positrons. The photons produced when these annihilate are measured.
126446.m: PET uses antimatter to make metabolic processes visible.

126447.q: What electric charge does an antiproton have?
126447.e: Antiparticles have the same mass but the opposite charge. The antiproton therefore carries the charge −1 e.
126447.m: Antiparticles have the opposite charge of their particle.

126448.q: How much energy is released when 1 g of antimatter annihilates completely with 1 g of matter, using c = 3 · 10^8 m/s?
126448.e: The entire mass of 2 g, so 0.002 kg, is converted. E = m · c² = 0.002 kg · 9 · 10^16 m²/s² = 1.8 · 10^14 J.
126448.m: In annihilation, the whole mass becomes energy according to Einstein’s formula.

126449.q: What did the ALPHA-g experiment at CERN show about antihydrogen in 2023?
a: It falls downwards in a gravitational field like normal matter
It rises upwards in a gravitational field
It is not affected by gravity at all
126449.e: The measurement confirmed that antimatter is attracted by gravity. This ruled out a repulsive “antigravity”.

126450.q: Which unsolved puzzle in physics concerns antimatter in the universe?
a: Why there is almost only matter and hardly any antimatter
Why antimatter is heavier than matter
Why antimatter only occurs on Earth
Why antimatter is slower than light
126450.e: In the Big Bang, matter and antimatter should really have been produced in equal amounts. Where the small excess of matter comes from has not yet been explained.
126450.m: Why the universe is made of matter is an open question.

126451.q: Where were neutrinos first detected directly in 1956?
126451.e: Clyde Cowan and Frederick Reines used the strong flow of neutrinos from a nuclear reactor in the USA. Reines later received the Nobel Prize for this.
126451.m: Neutrinos were first detected at a nuclear reactor in 1956.

126452.q: What does the observation of neutrino oscillations prove?
a: That neutrinos are faster than light
That there is only one kind of neutrino
126452.e: Neutrinos can change into another kind of neutrino along the way. This is only possible if they have a mass, even a tiny one. The Nobel Prize was awarded for this in 2015.
126452.m: Neutrino oscillations show that neutrinos have mass.

126453.q: Roughly how many neutrinos from the Sun hit one square centimetre of the Earth’s surface every second?
126453.e: Nuclear fusion in the Sun produces huge numbers of neutrinos. They pass through us all the time without us noticing anything.
126453.m: Every second, billions of solar neutrinos fly through our bodies.

126454.q: Where is the IceCube neutrino detector?
126454.e: IceCube uses a cubic kilometre of clear, deep Antarctic ice as a detector for high-energy neutrinos.
126454.m: The IceCube detector is buried in the ice of the South Pole.

126455.q: Which medium does the Super-Kamiokande detector in Japan use to detect neutrinos via Cherenkov light?
126455.e: A huge tank of ultra-pure water is surrounded by thousands of light sensors. Charged particles from neutrino reactions produce faint flashes of light in it.
126455.m: Super-Kamiokande looks for neutrinos in a huge water tank.

126456.q: What explained the apparently faster-than-light neutrinos sent from CERN to Gran Sasso in 2011?
a: A measuring error, partly caused by a badly fitted optical fibre connector
A mistake in the theory of relativity
126456.e: The OPERA experiment at first measured a flight time that was too short. Later, technical faults were found, and the neutrinos were not faster than light.
126456.m: Neutrinos are not faster than light either.

126457.q: Why do neutrinos pass through the whole Earth almost unhindered?
a: They are electrically neutral and only interact weakly
They are repelled by the Earth
They move more slowly than atoms
126457.e: Neutrinos feel neither the strong nor the electromagnetic force. That is why they react with matter only extremely rarely.
126457.m: Neutrinos hardly react with matter and fly straight through the Earth.

126458.q: During which event in 1987 were neutrinos from an exploding star measured for the first time?
a: During a meteorite impact in Siberia
During the flyby of Halley’s Comet
126458.e: The supernova in the Large Magellanic Cloud sent out a burst of neutrinos that was recorded by detectors in Japan and the USA.
126458.m: Supernova 1987A provided the first neutrinos from an exploding star.

126459.q: A proton passes through a voltage of 2000 V. How much kinetic energy does it gain?
126459.e: A particle with one elementary charge gains 1 eV per volt. At 2000 V, that is 2000 eV or 2 keV.
126459.m: One electronvolt is the energy of one elementary charge after one volt.

126460.q: Which former household appliance contained a small particle accelerator?
126460.e: In the picture tube, electrons were accelerated by a high voltage of several thousand volts and steered across the screen with magnetic fields.
126460.m: Old tube televisions were small electron accelerators.

126461.q: Who invented the cyclotron in the 1930s?
126461.e: In a cyclotron, particles spiral outwards in a magnetic field and are accelerated on each lap by an alternating electric field.
126461.m: Ernest Lawrence built the first cyclotron.

126462.q: Why are circular accelerators poorly suited for bringing electrons to the very highest energies?
a: On circular paths, electrons lose a lot of energy as synchrotron radiation
Electrons cannot be deflected by magnets
Electrons are too heavy for circular paths
126462.e: The radiation losses grow sharply with energy and are especially large for light particles. That is why linear accelerators tend to be used for very high electron energies.
126462.m: In a circular accelerator, light particles lose a lot of energy through radiation.

126463.q: Which facility at the Paul Scherrer Institute produces intense X-ray light with electrons on a circular path?
126463.e: The SLS is a synchrotron light source. The synchrotron radiation it deliberately produces is used, for example, to study materials and proteins.
126463.m: The Swiss Light Source uses synchrotron radiation for research.

126464.q: How are charged particles brought to higher energy in modern accelerators?
a: With electric fields in radio-frequency cavities
126464.e: Only electric fields can increase the energy of charged particles. Magnetic fields only change the direction of motion.
126464.m: Particles are accelerated by electric fields.

126465.q: What does the Paul Scherrer Institute also use accelerated protons for in medicine?
126465.e: Protons release their energy mainly at the end of their path. This allows tumours to be irradiated precisely while sparing the surrounding tissue.
126465.m: Protons can be used to irradiate tumours very precisely.

126466.q: Roughly what circumference is the Future Circular Collider (FCC) planned at CERN meant to have?
126466.e: The FCC would be more than three times as long as the LHC tunnel and would run under the Geneva area and France. No decision has yet been made on building it.
126466.m: The planned Future Circular Collider would be over three times as large as the LHC.

126467.q: At which research facility is the ATLAS particle detector?
a: At CERN’s Large Hadron Collider near Geneva
At the Paul Scherrer Institute in Villigen
126467.e: ATLAS is one of the large detectors at the LHC, CERN’s particle accelerator on the border between Switzerland and France. It records the collisions of protons.
126467.m: ATLAS is a detector at CERN’s LHC.

126468.q: Roughly how large is the ATLAS detector?
a: About 46 metres long and 25 metres high
About 4 metres long and 2 metres high
About 460 metres long and 250 metres high
About 15 metres long and 10 metres high
126468.e: ATLAS is about as tall as an eight-storey building and is considered the particle detector with the largest volume.
126468.m: ATLAS is the particle detector with the largest volume.

126469.q: Which long-sought particle did the ATLAS and CMS detectors detect in 2012?
126469.e: In 2012, ATLAS and CMS announced the discovery of the Higgs boson. It explains how elementary particles get their mass. The graviton has still not been detected.
126469.m: ATLAS and CMS discovered the Higgs boson in 2012.

126470.q: Why does the muon spectrometer form the outermost layer of ATLAS?
a: Because muons pass through the inner layers almost unhindered
Because muons are only produced outside the beam pipe
126470.e: Most other particles are stopped in the calorimeters. Muons get further and are therefore measured on the outside.
126470.m: Muons fly through almost everything, so they are measured right at the outside.

126471.q: What is the job of the calorimeters in the ATLAS detector?
a: To measure the energy of particles by stopping them
126471.e: In the calorimeters, particles produce showers whose total energy is measured. There are calorimeters for electrons and photons and for hadrons.
126471.m: Calorimeters measure the energy of particles.

126472.q: What is the ATLAS trigger system for?
a: It selects the interesting collisions to store in real time
It counts the visitors in the detector
126472.e: Far too many collisions take place every second to store them all. The trigger keeps only a small fraction of promising events.
126472.m: The trigger decides in a flash which collisions are stored.

126473.q: How does ATLAS detect particles such as neutrinos that leave the detector unnoticed?
a: Through missing momentum at right angles to the beam direction
Through their tracks in the inner detector
Through flashes of light in the magnets
126473.e: Before the collision, the particles have no total momentum at right angles to the beam. If momentum in this direction is missing afterwards, an invisible particle must have carried it away.
126473.m: Invisible particles give themselves away through missing momentum.

126474.q: How does the ATLAS inner detector measure the momentum of charged particles?
a: Through the curvature of their tracks in the magnetic field
Through the colour of their light
Through the sound of the impact
126474.e: A magnetic field bends charged particles onto curved paths. The greater their momentum, the weaker the curvature.
126474.m: The less a track is curved, the greater the particle’s momentum.

126475.q: What was the name of the first web browser, which Tim Berners-Lee programmed at CERN in 1990?
126475.e: The first browser was also an editor with which web pages could be edited. To avoid confusion with the web itself, it was later renamed Nexus.
126475.m: The first web browser was called WorldWideWeb.

126476.q: In which year did Tim Berners-Lee submit his first proposal for a networked information system at CERN?
126476.e: In March 1989 he wrote “Information Management: A Proposal”. His supervisor wrote “vague but exciting” on it.
126476.m: The World Wide Web began in 1989 with a proposal at CERN.

126477.q: Which Belgian computer scientist worked closely with Tim Berners-Lee at CERN on developing the web?
126477.e: In 1990, Robert Cailliau revised the project proposal with Berners-Lee and promoted the web at CERN.
126477.m: Robert Cailliau helped Tim Berners-Lee build the web.

126478.q: On which type of computer did the first web server at CERN run?
126478.e: Berners-Lee used a NeXT workstation. A note stuck on the machine said that it should not be switched off.
126478.m: The first web server ran on a NeXT computer at CERN.

126479.q: At which address could the world’s first website be reached?
126479.e: The page explained the World Wide Web project itself. CERN later restored it at the old address.
126479.m: The world’s first website was info.cern.ch.

126480.q: What did CERN decide about the World Wide Web in 1993?
a: To release the software to everyone without licence fees
To sell the web to a company
To allow the web only for physicists
126480.e: Because the web was free to use, companies and private individuals could use it at no cost. This contributed greatly to how quickly it spread.
126480.m: In 1993, CERN made the web available to everyone free of charge.

126481.q: What was the World Wide Web originally developed for at CERN?
126481.e: Thousands of researchers from all over the world worked with different computers. The web was meant to make documents easily accessible through hyperlinks.
126481.m: The web was meant to help researchers share information.

126482.q: Which markup language for web pages did Tim Berners-Lee develop at CERN?
126482.e: Hypertext Markup Language is used to describe the structure of web pages and set links. He also developed the transfer protocol HTTP and web addresses (URLs).
126482.m: Web pages are described with the language HTML.

126483.q: Which Swiss astronomer concluded in 1933 from observations of the Coma galaxy cluster that there must be invisible “dark matter”?
126483.e: Zwicky found that the galaxies in the cluster move too fast to be held together by the visible mass alone.
126483.m: Fritz Zwicky coined the term dark matter in 1933.

126484.q: According to current measurements, roughly what share of the total energy content of the universe does dark matter make up?
126484.e: According to measurements of the cosmic background radiation, the universe consists mostly of dark energy and dark matter. Dark matter contributes a good quarter.
126484.m: Dark matter makes up about a quarter of the universe.

126485.q: Roughly how many times more dark matter than ordinary matter is there in the universe?
126485.e: The measurements give a ratio of about five to one. So stars, gas, planets and we ourselves are only a small part of the matter.
126485.m: There is about five times more dark matter than ordinary matter.

126486.q: Which observation by Vera Rubin in the 1970s supported the existence of dark matter?
a: The measurement of the cosmic background radiation
126486.e: Stars at the edge of galaxies orbit almost as fast as those further in. This can only be explained by extra, invisible mass.
126486.m: Fast-orbiting stars at the edge of galaxies reveal dark matter.

126487.q: Which effect can be used to map the distribution of dark matter?
126487.e: Mass curves space and bends the light of galaxies behind it. From the distortions, the mass can be worked out even if it is invisible.
126487.m: Gravitational lenses make invisible mass visible.

126488.q: What does the abbreviation WIMP, a possible candidate for dark matter, stand for?
126488.e: WIMPs would be heavy particles that interact only weakly with ordinary matter. Despite sensitive detectors, none have been found so far.
126488.m: WIMPs are hypothetical heavy particles of dark matter.

a: Because it does not emit, absorb or reflect light
Because it only appears at night
Because it only occurs in black holes
126489.e: Dark matter only reveals itself through its gravity. As far as we know today, it does not interact with electromagnetic radiation.
126489.m: Dark matter is invisible and only shows itself through gravity.

126490.q: Which ESA space telescope, launched in 2023, is meant to map the distribution of dark matter and dark energy?
126490.e: Euclid observes billions of galaxies and measures their shapes and distances. From this, the distribution of dark matter in the cosmos can be reconstructed.
126490.m: The ESA telescope Euclid explores the dark universe.

126491.q: In which city did the naturalist Conrad Gessner work as town physician in the 16th century?
126491.e: Conrad Gessner was town physician of Zurich and also taught natural history there. He is one of the most important all-round scholars of the Swiss Renaissance.
126491.m: Conrad Gessner was town physician in Zurich.

126492.q: Which work by Conrad Gessner in several volumes is considered the foundation of modern zoology?
126492.e: In the “Historia animalium”, Gessner brought together the knowledge of his time about animals and added his own observations and woodcuts. The work appeared in several volumes from 1551.
126492.m: Gessner’s animal book “Historia animalium” founded modern zoology.

a: An atlas of the Alpine passes
126493.e: In it, Gessner listed thousands of works in Latin, Greek and Hebrew with their authors and contents. That is why he is considered the father of bibliography.
126493.m: With the “Bibliotheca universalis”, Gessner became the father of bibliography.

126494.q: Which parts of plants did Conrad Gessner consider especially important for classifying plants?
126494.e: Gessner realised early on that flowers, fruits and seeds show related plants better than leaf shape or usefulness. This idea later became the basis of botanical classification.
126494.m: Gessner recognised the value of flowers and fruits for classifying plants.

126495.q: Which mountain near Lucerne did Conrad Gessner climb in 1555 and describe in a separate text?
126495.e: In 1555 Gessner climbed Pilatus and described the climb and the plant life. He is therefore seen as an early example of someone climbing mountains for the joy of nature.

126496.q: Which epidemic disease did Conrad Gessner die of in Zurich in 1565?
126496.e: As town physician, Gessner cared for the sick during a wave of plague and caught it himself. He died in 1565 at the age of 49.
126496.m: Conrad Gessner died of the plague in 1565.

126497.q: Which plant family, which also includes the African violet, is named after Conrad Gessner?
126497.e: The genus Gesneria, and with it the gesneriad family (Gesneriaceae), honours Conrad Gessner. Many of its species grow in the tropics.
126497.m: The gesneriad family bears the name of Conrad Gessner.

126498.q: On which banknote of the sixth Swiss banknote series (from 1976) was Conrad Gessner shown?
126498.e: The National Bank’s sixth banknote series showed well-known figures from science and culture. Gessner appeared on the 50-franc note.
126498.m: Conrad Gessner was shown on the former 50-franc note.
